title: Brutalist Architecture

paragraphs.text: The concrete exteriors of brutalist architecture can exhibit a tough, unsympathetic and aggressive style. Its unconventional shapes, many entrances and multiple levels are hard to understand, making it a style that is difficult to love. It takes time to recognise the value of this architecture; it's like a difficult modern novel or piece of abstract classical music. Though, as with all these cultural styles. Once you've cracked the code you can find yourself admiring brutalism much more than something more commonplace.

By 1952, Le Corbusier's Unite d'Habitation, in Marseille, France, had become one of the best-known examples of this style of architecture, but over time, dozens of buildings would rival this block of flats. However, it wasn't until the 1960s that brutalism really accelerated and became an important global architectural movement. Spurred on by the advent of cheap flights, cheap fuels, globe-trotting architects and lavish photography of the buildings in new colour magazines, the style spread extensively.

In the popular mindset, brutalism became associated with communism. Concrete buildings — the flats and more importantly, the public buildings such as hospitals and universities — were the living embodiment of a new society. But this wasn't just a style favoured in communist countries — it turned up in the heart of the US too. A new map published by a media company in the US shows dozens of brutalist buildings in Washington DC, most notably its incredible Metro stations. It wasn't always the architecture of the government buildings either — there are brutalist insurance offices in Chicago and other cities, and some dazzling churches by the German architect Gottfried Böhm across West Germany.

For the British academic Barnabas Calder, whose book Row Concrete offers a lively history, brutalism was the highpoint of architecture. 'There will never be another time when architects can be so free to express themselves,' he argues, 'when energy prices are so low that concrete can be churned out and stretched into fantastical shapes.' Cultural commentator Jonathan Meades talks about architects' contempt for the critics in the 1960s, designing with a free hand, providing buildings that were remarkable, singular and most importantly, that had no precedent. Brutalism shocked the establishment, prodded and provoked precisely because it was so different. This radicalism, in turn, produced a kind of hatred; over the years, the hatred has grown and many brutalist buildings have been knocked down. But this radicalism is what has made fans of the style so passionate.

It is true that brutalist buildings were sometimes cheap to build, but what's often overlooked is that they were created by real craftsmen who knew how to make the concrete set, and how to finish the whole thing off. Artists, including William Mitchell, put wonderful cubist concrete murals on the outside of many buildings and in pedestrian subways under motorways.

Critics from the Northern Hemisphere have tended to ignore the Australian and New Zealand architecture of the 20th century, while Australia and New Zealand have been unsure exactly what they ended up with — aside from a lot of extremely odd buildings. But what both countries have is a rich repository of brutalism, from the University of Auckland's campus and the Beehive Parliament Building in Wellington, to the Roeder's Digest printing works in Sydney. As described by Australian art critic Robert Hughes in his TV series, Australian brutalist buildings shock because they are raw and austere — and were meant to be. The National Gallery and High Court of Australia in Canberra, both Immense, powerful places of brutalist architecture, were supposed to be part of a huge raised plaza eventually linking to a new Parliament House. But Canberra put its parliament elsewhere and the project was never completed.

Sadly, demolition has become an uncomfortable fact of life for many brutalist buildings in the 21st century. Recently, though, the tide has turned. The National Trust of Australia has stepped in to save the School of Molecular Bioscience at the University of Sydney, just as campaigners have fought for the Birmingham Library in the UK and for Paul Rudolph's Orange County Government Center in upstate New York. Félix Torkar and Oliver Elser, fans of brutalism who work at the Deutsches Architekturmuseum in Frankfurt, designed the 2016 German Pavilion at the Venice Biennale in the brutalist style. One building that will remain standing is the Hayward Gallery in London thanks to Britain's National Trust that has organised tours for the public.

Brutalism has been synonymous with dystopia but it can also be about utopia: it can be surprisingly welcoming. The architects who designed it wanted it to be a declaration of love for cites, not hate. Although these buildings may seem weird to us, thousands of people live and work in them every day. They're the most abnormal of shapes and yet they are the backdrop for the most normal of lives. Brutalism will never be commonplace; It will always live on as one of the most dramatic styles of architecture we ever developed, a tribute to our abilities and inventiveness as humans.
